pos: n. (the wife of a father's brother; a relation named in the law of forbidden degrees)
etymology: From Latin amita, a father's sister, through Old French ante. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Leviticus 18, naming the wife of a father's brother as one of the near kin a man may not approach.
biblical_def: Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's brother, thou shalt not approach to his wife: she is thine aunt. The verse belongs to the chapter that defines the forbidden degrees of marriage, and the chapter opens with a principle rather than a list: none of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD. Then the relations are enumerated one by one, mother, father's wife, sister, granddaughter, aunt, daughter in law, brother's wife, and the rest, so that no household could plead ignorance. The chapter grounds all of it in the character of God and the history of the nations: defile not ye yourselves in any of these things, for in all these the nations are defiled which I cast out before you. The land itself is said to vomit out its inhabitants for these practices. And the chapter closes by naming them abominable customs, with the command, therefore shall ye keep mine ordinance, that ye commit not any one of these abominable customs, which were committed before you. The sexual law is covenant law, national in its consequences, and rooted in who God is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the sister of one's father or mother, and correlatively the wife of one's uncle; in Scripture, a relation within the forbidden degrees.
webster_full: AUNT, n. The sister of one's father or mother; correlative to nephew or niece.
KINDRED, n. Relation by birth; consanguinity; relatives by blood.
AFFINITY, n. The relation contracted by marriage, between a husband and his wife's kindred.
INCEST, n. The crime of cohabitation or sexual commerce between persons related within the degrees wherein marriage is prohibited.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action.
scriptures: Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's brother, thou shalt not approach to his wife: she is thine aunt.
Lev 18:6
None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD.
Defile not ye yourselves in any of these things: for in all these the nations are defiled which I cast out before you:
Therefore shall ye keep mine ordinance, that ye commit not any one of these abominable customs, which were committed before you, and that ye defile not yourselves therein: I am the LORD your God.
corruption_summary: Sexual boundaries are treated as private arrangements between consenting adults with no bearing on anyone else; Leviticus 18 grounds them in God's character, assigns them to households, and attaches national consequences.
corruption_paragraphs: The consent framework is the governing sexual ethic of the age, and Leviticus 18 was written against its ancestor. The chapter does not ask whether the parties agreed. It names relations, fixes limits by kinship and covenant, and repeats I am the LORD like a refrain through the whole catalogue, because the authority for the limit is the Lawgiver and not the participants. The same chapter goes on to name the sacrifice of children to Molech and homosexual practice and bestiality in the same list and under the same sanction, and calls the whole set abominations for which the land spued out its inhabitants.

The corruption in the church takes the softer form of treating these chapters as ceremonial and therefore obsolete. The New Testament does not read them that way. Paul dealt with a case at Corinth of a man having his father's wife — a Leviticus 18 offence — and treated it as fornication not so much as named among the Gentiles, requiring discipline. The moral law binds still, the household is still the unit God addresses, and the dictionary holds marriage to be one man and one woman covenanting before God for life, within the degrees Scripture permits.
roots_summary: Hebrew dodah (H1733), an aunt, the wife of a father's brother; she'er (H7607), flesh, and so near kin; to'ebah (H8441), abomination.
roots_lines: Hebrew dodah (H1733) — an aunt, the wife of an uncle; she is thine aunt.
Hebrew dowd (H1730) — an uncle, a beloved one; thy father's brother.
Hebrew she'er (H7607) — flesh, and so blood relation; any that is near of kin.
Hebrew to'ebah (H8441) — an abomination, a detested thing; these abominable customs.
Hebrew chuqqah (H2708) — an ordinance, a statute; therefore shall ye keep mine ordinance.
usage: “thou shalt not approach to his wife: she is thine aunt” — the single occurrence.
“None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin” — the principle of the chapter.
“I am the LORD” — the refrain that supplies the authority.

pos: n. (a kinswoman; the Authorized Version's word for Elisabeth's relation to Mary)
etymology: From Latin consobrinus, a mother's sister's child, through Old French; in older English it covered kindred generally, not the narrow modern sense. The Authorized Version uses it of Elisabeth, where the Greek means simply kinswoman.
biblical_def: And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren. Gabriel has just announced to Mary a conception with no human father, and the sign he gives her is a second impossible conception in her own family. The two are joined by the sentence that follows and that governs both: for with God nothing shall be impossible. Mary's answer is the great model of faith under an unimaginable word: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. She went with haste into the hill country, and the meeting of the two women is one of the most charged scenes in the Gospels: when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb, and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost. An unborn John recognised an unborn Christ. Everything the dictionary holds about the personhood of the unborn is in that verse without an argument being made, and Mary's song follows, beginning with a soul that magnifies the Lord and a spirit that rejoices in God her Saviour.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the son or daughter of an uncle or aunt; formerly used for any kinsman, in which broader sense the Authorized Version uses it of Elisabeth.
webster_full: COUSIN, n. The son or daughter of an uncle or aunt; the children of brothers and sisters being usually denominated cousins.
COUSIN, n. In a more general sense, a kinsman or kinswoman; a relative.
KINSWOMAN, n. A female relation.
BARREN, a. Not prolific; not bearing children; applied to females.
ANNUNCIATION, n. The tidings brought by the angel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary.
scriptures: Luk 1:36
And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren.
Luk 1:37
For with God nothing shall be impossible.
Luk 1:38
And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her.
Luk 1:41
And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost:
corruption_summary: The virgin birth is treated as legend or as a dispensable symbol, and the unborn as something less than a person; Luke presents both as facts investigated and set in order, with two unborn children meeting in one room.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke states his method at the head of the Gospel: having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, that thou mightest know the certainty of those things wherein thou hast been instructed. That is the language of investigation, not of legend. The virgin conception is not a decorative miracle attached to a moral teacher; it is how God the Son entered his own creation, and the Chalcedonian confession of one Person in two natures rests on it. Mary's own question — how shall this be, seeing I know not a man — shows she understood exactly what was being said and that it was not ordinary.

The second doctrine in the passage is delivered without a word of argument. The babe leaped in her womb, and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost. John, six months before birth, responds to the presence of Christ, days after conception. Scripture is consistent on this from the Psalms — thou didst cover me in my mother's womb; thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect — to Jeremiah, who was known and sanctified before he came forth. The image of God is not conferred at some later threshold. It is there from the beginning, and the Lord of glory himself once had a gestational age.
roots_summary: Greek suggenes (G4773), a kinsman or kinswoman; sullambano (G4815), to conceive; adunateo (G101), to be impossible.
roots_lines: Greek suggenes (G4773) — of the same kin, a relative; rendered cousin at Luke 1:36.
Greek sullambano (G4815) — to conceive, to take together; she hath also conceived a son.
Greek steira (G4723) — barren, sterile; who was called barren.
Greek adunateo (G101) — to be impossible; with God nothing shall be impossible.
Greek brephos (G1025) — an infant, a babe, born or unborn; the babe leaped in her womb.
usage: “thy cousin Elisabeth” — the single occurrence, where the Greek means kinswoman.
“For with God nothing shall be impossible” — the word that joins the two conceptions.
“the babe leaped in her womb” — one unborn child answering another.

pos: n. (the office of chief butler or cupbearer to Pharaoh)
etymology: From butler, Old French bouteillier, a bottle-bearer, with the ending -ship denoting office. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the office Pharaoh restored to the chief butler on his birthday, exactly as Joseph had interpreted.
biblical_def: And he restored the chief butler unto his butlership again; and he gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand. The dream had been of three branches budding, blossoming, and bringing forth ripe grapes, and the butler pressing them into Pharaoh's cup; Joseph read it in three days and asked one thing in return: think on me when it shall be well with thee, and make mention of me unto Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house. The next verse is one of the flattest and most painful in Genesis: yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him. Two full years passed. Then Pharaoh dreamed, and the memory returned with an apology that is really an excuse: I do remember my faults this day. What the reader is meant to see is that the delay was not an accident of a servant's bad memory. Had Joseph been released at once he would have gone home a freed prisoner; kept two more years, he came out of the dungeon on the exact morning Egypt needed an interpreter, and stood before Pharaoh. Joseph himself gave the doctrine at the end: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the office of a butler; in Scripture, the office of the chief cupbearer restored by Pharaoh on the third day, as Joseph foretold.
webster_full: BUTLER, n. A servant or officer in a family whose principal business is to take charge of the liquors, plate, etc.
BUTLERSHIP, n. The office of a butler.
CUPBEARER, n. An attendant of a prince or at a feast, who conveys wine or other liquors to the guests.
INTERPRET, v.t. To explain the meaning of words to a person who does not understand them.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: And he restored the chief butler unto his butlership again; and he gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand:
Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.
Gen 41:9
Then spake the chief butler unto Pharaoh, saying, I do remember my faults this day:
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
corruption_summary: Delay is read as divine absence or as the failure of the people who forgot us; Genesis presents two forgotten years as the precise interval that placed Joseph before Pharaoh on the right morning.
corruption_paragraphs: The theology of Genesis 40 to 41 lies in the joint between two chapters. Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him — and then, it came to pass at the end of two full years, that Pharaoh dreamed. The forgetting is a real sin of ingratitude and is named as such, and it is also the instrument by which the timing was arranged. Scripture does not soften either half. Men act freely and often badly, and God's purpose runs through their acting without excusing it, which is the doctrine of concurrence the Reformed confessions state and which Joseph puts in ten words at the end of his life.

This is the answer to the modern reading of hard providence as either divine indifference or a problem to be explained away. Joseph was sold, lied about, imprisoned, and forgotten, and the LORD was with Joseph in every chapter of it, a phrase Genesis repeats deliberately in the pit, in Potiphar's house, and in the prison. The comfort is not that the suffering was small but that it was not loose. Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
roots_summary: Hebrew mashqeh (H4945), a butler or cupbearer, from shaqah, to give drink; zakar (H2142), to remember; shakach (H7911), to forget.

Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, to restore; he restored the chief butler.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, to mark; think on me when it shall be well with thee.
Hebrew shakach (H7911) — to forget, to mislay; but forgat him.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, to devise, to reckon; ye thought evil, but God meant it unto good.

“yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him” — the two silent years.
“but God meant it unto good” — the doctrine Joseph drew from it.

pos: n. (compulsory labour exacted as tribute; the levy Solomon laid on the remnant of the Canaanites)
etymology: From bond, a fetter or obligation, and service. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the tribute Solomon levied on the peoples left in the land, distinguished in the next verse from what he did with Israelites.
biblical_def: Their children that were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel also were not able utterly to destroy, upon those did Solomon levy a tribute of bondservice unto this day. The Chronicler-like care of the next verse matters: but of the children of Israel did Solomon make no bondmen; but they were men of war, and his servants, and his princes, and his captains, and rulers of his chariots, and his horsemen. Whatever Solomon did with the remnant of the nations, the covenant people were not made slaves — and yet the story does not end there. When Rehoboam came to Shechem, the complaint of the ten tribes was precisely about the burden: thy father made our yoke grievous; now therefore make thou the grievous service of thy father, and his heavy yoke which he put upon us, lighter, and we will serve thee. Rehoboam took the young men's counsel, promised to add to the yoke, and lost ten tribes in an afternoon. The New Testament takes the whole vocabulary of yokes and bondage and settles it in one verse: stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): slavery; the condition of a bond servant; in Scripture, the compulsory labour Solomon levied on the remnant of the Canaanite nations.
webster_full: BONDSERVICE, n. The condition of a bond servant; slavery.
BONDMAN, n. A man slave, or one bound to service without wages.
TRIBUTE, n. An annual or stated sum of money paid by one prince or nation to another.
YOKE, n. Something that binds or connects; a mark of servitude; slavery; bondage.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; in a religious sense, freedom from the bondage of sin and from the ceremonial law.
scriptures: Their children that were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel also were not able utterly to destroy, upon those did Solomon levy a tribute of bondservice unto this day.
But of the children of Israel did Solomon make no bondmen: but they were men of war, and his servants, and his princes, and his captains, and rulers of his chariots, and his horsemen.
Thy father made our yoke grievous: now therefore make thou the grievous service of thy father, and his heavy yoke which he put upon us, lighter, and we will serve thee.
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
corruption_summary: Scripture's record of servitude is read either as divine endorsement of chattel slavery or as proof the Bible is worthless on the subject; the texts distinguish carefully between forms of service and press toward the liberty Christ purchased.
corruption_paragraphs: Two bad readings meet here. The first takes any biblical mention of servitude as approval of the race-based chattel slavery of the modern era — a system the Bible condemns at its root, since Exodus makes manstealing a capital crime and 1 Timothy lists menstealers with murderers and perjurers among those the law is made for. The second discards the Scriptures as compromised. Both skip the actual text, which regulates existing servitude with release years, sabbath rest for servants, protection from mutilation, and refuge for the runaway, and which draws a line here between the levy on the nations and the treatment of Israelites.

The New Testament's trajectory is unmistakable to anyone who reads Philemon. Paul sends a runaway back not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, and tells the master to receive him as myself. He tells servants to serve heartily as to the Lord and masters to give what is just and equal, knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven. And he tells the servant who can be made free to use it rather. The gospel does not bless the yoke; it undermines it, and it begins by naming the deepest bondage, which is sin, and the liberty Christ bought from it.

“of the children of Israel did Solomon make no bondmen” — the distinction drawn.
“be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” — where the whole vocabulary lands.

pos: n. (the hour of eating; the moment Boaz called Ruth to the table)
etymology: From meal, Old English mael, a measure or fixed time, and time. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the field of Boaz, when the owner invited a foreign gleaner to sit among the reapers and eat.
biblical_def: And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left. Every detail is a step across a boundary. Ruth is a Moabitess, a widow, and a gleaner — entitled by the law of Leviticus to follow the reapers and gather what they drop, and entitled to nothing else. Boaz has already told his young men not to touch her and to let fall handfuls on purpose. Now he calls her from the edge of the field to the middle of the meal, seats her beside the reapers, and hands her food himself. The blessing he had spoken over her a few verses earlier names what is happening: the LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust. And Naomi, hearing whose field it was, sees further than either of them: the man is near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen. The mealtime is the first movement of a redemption that ends in a marriage, a son, and the line of David.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the usual time of eating meals; in Scripture, the hour at which Boaz called Ruth from gleaning to sit among the reapers.
webster_full: MEALTIME, n. The usual time of eating meals.
GLEAN, v.t. To gather the stalks and ears of grain which reapers leave behind them.
REAPER, n. One that cuts grain with a sickle.
KINSMAN, n. A man of the same race or family; one related by blood.
REDEEM, v.t. To purchase back; to ransom; to liberate or rescue from captivity or bondage.
scriptures: Rut 2:14

And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left.
Rut 2:12
The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.
Rut 2:20

And Naomi said unto her daughter in law, Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead. And Naomi said unto her, The man is near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen. one
Rut 4:14
And the women said unto Naomi, Blessed be the LORD, which hath not left thee this day without a kinsman, that his name may be famous in Israel.
corruption_summary: Care for the poor is reduced to a transfer of goods at arm's length, when the law of gleaning required the poor to work the field and Boaz's kindness brought a foreign widow to the table.
corruption_paragraphs: The gleaning law is one of the wisest arrangements in Scripture and it satisfies neither modern instinct. It is not a handout: the corners of the field and the dropped sheaves are left, and the poor must come and work all day to gather them, as Ruth did from morning until evening. Nor is it a market: the owner has no right to the corners at all, since God reserved them, and Leviticus signs the command with I am the LORD your God. Dignity and obligation are held together. The poor eat by their own labour, and the landowner obeys a law rather than dispensing a favour.

Boaz then does more than the law requires, which is where the book becomes a picture of something larger. He commands handfuls of purpose, he protects her from the young men, he calls her to the meal, he answers her at the threshing floor with the kinsman's redemption, and he pays the price at the gate in public. That is the pattern of a redeemer: near kin, able to redeem, and willing. The women of Bethlehem said it at the end over a child in Naomi's lap — blessed be the LORD, which hath not left thee this day without a kinsman.

“under whose wings thou art come to trust” — the blessing Boaz had already spoken.
“The man is near of kin unto us” — what Naomi saw in it.

pos: n. pl. (the rowers' seats or the deck of a ship; made of ivory in Ezekiel's Tyre)
etymology: Old English benc, a long seat. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in the lament over Tyrus, where the ship-city's benches are made of ivory brought out of the isles of Chittim.
biblical_def: Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim. Ezekiel's lament over Tyre is built on a single extended figure: the merchant city is a ship, and the prophet builds her plank by plank out of the best of every nation — fir trees of Senir for boards, a cedar from Lebanon for a mast, oaks of Bashan for oars, fine linen of Egypt for a sail, benches of ivory. Then he crews her, names her merchants nation by nation, loads her, and sinks her: thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, and all thy men of war shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin. The city had said, I am of perfect beauty. The chapter after it addresses the prince of Tyrus, whose heart was lifted up so that he said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas — and answers, yet thou art a man, and not God. John saw the same ship go down at the end of the Bible, and the merchants of the earth weeping over her.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a long seat, usually of board or plank; in a ship, the rowers' seats; in Scripture, the ivory benches of the ship-city Tyre.
webster_full: BENCH, n. A long seat, usually of board or plank, differing from a stool in its greater length.
IVORY, n. The tusk of an elephant, a hard, solid substance, of a fine white color.
OAR, n. An instrument for rowing boats, being a piece of timber round or square at one end.
MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.
LUXURY, n. A free or extravagant indulgence in the pleasures of the table; voluptuousness.
scriptures: Eze 27:6
Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim.
Eze 27:3
And say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea, which art a merchant of the people for many isles, Thus saith the Lord GOD; O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty.

Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that are in thee, and in all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin.
And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:
corruption_summary: Commercial power is treated as a neutral engine rather than a spiritual condition; Ezekiel builds Tyre out of the world's best materials, and then names the pride at the centre of it and sinks the whole ship.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 27 is the most detailed picture of international trade in Scripture, and its tone is not hostility to commerce. The prophet takes evident pleasure in the craftsmanship — the fir boards, the cedar mast, the Bashan oars, the ivory benches, the blue and purple from the isles of Elishah. What he indicts is the self-estimate: O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty. A city can be genuinely excellent and genuinely damned, and the excellence is what makes the boast plausible. The judgment falls not because trade is wicked but because the traders had made a god of the trading.

Revelation 18 deliberately reuses Ezekiel's cargo list — gold, silver, precious stones, fine linen, ivory, cinnamon, and at the end of it slaves, and souls of men — and sets the merchants of the earth weeping over a fallen Babylon because no man buyeth their merchandise any more. That last item in the manifest is the tell. An economy that will trade in men has arrived where Tyre arrived, and the church's word to it is the one the angel gives: Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins.

Hebrew rekullah (H7404) — traffick, merchandise; the recurring noun of the chapter.

pos: n. pl. (cells or vaulted chambers of a prison)
etymology: From Old French cabane, a hut or small chamber. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, of the cells in the dungeon where Jeremiah was imprisoned in the house of Jonathan the scribe.
biblical_def: When Jeremiah was entered into the dungeon, and into the cabins, and Jeremiah had remained there many days. He had been arrested at the gate of Benjamin on a false charge of defecting to the Chaldeans, beaten by the princes, and put in the house of Jonathan the scribe, which had been made a prison. What follows is one of the strangest interviews in Scripture. Then Zedekiah the king sent, and took him out, and the king asked him secretly in his house, and said, Is there any word from the LORD? And Jeremiah said, There is: for, said he, thou shalt be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon. A king who has just imprisoned a prophet sends for him in private to ask whether God has spoken, and receives the same sentence he was trying to suppress, from a beaten man who had every reason to soften it. Jeremiah then asks not to be sent back to that house lest he die there. Later they let him down with cords into a miry dungeon where he sank in the mire. Paul's summary of the whole matter was written from a Roman chain: I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a small room or cell; an apartment in a ship for officers; in Scripture, the cells of the dungeon where Jeremiah was held many days.
webster_full: CABIN, n. A small room; an inclosed place; a cottage or hut.
DUNGEON, n. A close prison, or a deep dark place of confinement.
PRISON, n. A place of confinement; a jail; a place where persons are restrained of liberty.
PERSECUTION, n. The infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
FIDELITY, n. Faithfulness; firm adherence to duty or to truth.
scriptures: When Jeremiah was entered into the dungeon, and into the cabins, and Jeremiah had remained there many days;

Then Zedekiah the king sent, and took him out: and the king asked him secretly in his house, and said, Is there any word from the LORD? And Jeremiah said, There is: for, said he, thou shalt be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.
Jer 38:6

Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
corruption_summary: A prophet's message is expected to soften under pressure, and a preacher's faithfulness is measured by the reception he gets; Jeremiah repeated the identical sentence to the king who had jailed him, and was sent back to the cells.
corruption_paragraphs: Zedekiah's secret question is the portrait of a man who wants the word of God to be different rather than wanting God. He asks privately because he fears the princes; he keeps Jeremiah alive because he half believes him; he will not act on anything he hears. And Jeremiah, who could have bought his freedom with one softened clause, gives the same answer he had given in the street. The measure of a ministry is not whether the hearer changes but whether the message did.

The cost is recorded without romance. Jeremiah asks the king plainly not to send him back to Jonathan's house, lest I die there — a prophet may ask for mercy and there is no shame in it. He is later let down by cords into a dungeon with no water but mire, and sinks in it, and is pulled out by an Ethiopian eunuch with old cast clouts and rotten rags put under his armholes. Scripture keeps such details because the faithfulness it commends is not stoicism. He wept, he complained to God in language that would alarm most congregations, and he did not change the message.

“Is there any word from the LORD? And Jeremiah said, There is” — the answer unchanged.
“but the word of God is not bound” — Paul from his own chain.

pos: n. pl. (polished brass mirrors; the metal of the laver)
etymology: From looking and glass; ancient mirrors were polished bronze rather than glass. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, of the mirrors the women gave, out of which the laver of the tabernacle was made.
biblical_def: And he made the laver of brass, and the foot of it of brass, of the lookingglasses of the women assembling, which assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. The detail is easy to miss and impossible to forget once seen. The laver stood between the altar and the tent, and the priests washed their hands and their feet there before they went in to minister, that they die not. The brass it was made of had been mirrors — the instruments by which women had looked at themselves, surrendered and melted down into a basin in which priests looked at nothing but water and washed. Exodus 30 gives the laver's purpose and its warning together. James takes up the mirror on the other side: if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass, who beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was. The word is the mirror that shows a man truly, and the danger is walking away from it. Paul sets the last word beyond this life: for now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a mirror; a glass which reflects the form of the person who looks on it; in Scripture, the polished brass of the women, made into the laver.
webster_full: LOOKING-GLASS, n. A glass which reflects the form of the person who looks on it; a mirror.
LAVER, n. A vessel for washing; a large basin; in the temple service, a basin placed in the court for the priests to wash in.
BRASS, n. An alloy of copper and zinc; in Scripture, generally copper or bronze.
MIRROR, n. A looking glass; any polished substance that forms images by the reflection of rays of light.
SELF-EXAMINATION, n. An examination or inquiry into one's own state, conduct and motives.
scriptures: Exo 38:8
And he made the laver of brass, and the foot of it of brass, of the lookingglasses of the women assembling, which assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.
Thou shalt also make a laver of brass, and his foot also of brass, to wash withal: and thou shalt put it between the tabernacle of the congregation and the altar, and thou shalt put water therein.
Jas 1:23
For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass:
For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
corruption_summary: Self-examination is replaced by self-esteem on one side and by self-loathing on the other; the laver made out of mirrors turns the instrument of self-regard into a vessel for cleansing, which is the biblical direction of looking.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern self takes its readings from the mirror, whether the verdict returned is flattering or crushing, and both verdicts come from the same instrument and the same authority. Exodus melts the instrument down. The brass that had shown women their own faces becomes the basin in which priests wash before they approach God, and what a man sees there is the water and his own need of it. That is the biblical order of self-knowledge: we learn what we are in the presence of God and not in front of ourselves. Isaiah did not know he was a man of unclean lips until he saw the Lord high and lifted up.

James supplies the practical warning and it is about memory. A man looks into the perfect law of liberty, sees himself truly, and goes his way and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was. Hearing without doing is not a lesser obedience; it is the specific mechanism of self-deception, and James says so — deceiving your own selves. The remedy is not more intense looking but continuing in the law and doing the work, and the promise attached is that this man shall be blessed in his deed.
roots_summary: Hebrew mar'ah (H4759), a mirror or vision, from ra'ah, to see; kiyowr (H3595), a laver or basin; rachats (H7364), to wash.

“beholding his natural face in a glass” — James's hearer who forgets.

pos: n. (a round drinking bowl without a handle)
etymology: From Old French gobelet, a small cup. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the Song, in the bridegroom's description of his bride.
biblical_def: Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies. The Song of Solomon is a canonical book of married love, and its frankness is deliberate. The dictionary takes it in the plain sense first — a husband praising his wife's body in language of plenty, a cup that is never empty and a harvest heap ringed with flowers — and then in the covenantal sense the whole book carries, since Scripture uses marriage from Genesis to Revelation as the figure of Christ and his church. The book's own summary of the relation is the line the bride speaks a few verses later: I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me. That belonging is mutual, exclusive, and delighted, and it is the same shape as the covenant. Proverbs gives the plain counsel in the same register: let thy fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of thy youth. And Paul gives the command that governs a Christian husband and sets the cost of it: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a kind of cup or drinking vessel, without a handle; in Scripture, the bridegroom's figure in the Song of Solomon.
webster_full: GOBLET, n. A kind of cup or drinking vessel, without a handle.
BRIDEGROOM, n. A man newly married; or a man about to be married.
SPOUSE, n. A man or woman engaged or joined in wedlock; a married person.
CONJUGAL, a. Belonging to marriage; suitable or appropriate to the marriage state.
TYPE, n. A sign; a symbol; a figure of something to come.
scriptures: Sng 7:2
Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies.
Sng 7:10
I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.
Pro 5:18
Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.
Eph 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
corruption_summary: The Song is either allegorised until nothing bodily remains in it, or read as a celebration of desire detached from covenant; it is a canonical book about a husband and a wife, and about Christ and the church, and it will not release either sense.
corruption_paragraphs: The older allegorising tradition was embarrassed by the book and read every line as doctrine with no marriage left in it. The modern reading keeps the body and drops the covenant, taking the Song as a celebration of erotic feeling as such. Both lose something the text insists on. The Song is unmistakably about a man and a woman, and it is placed in a canon where marriage is from the first the joining of one man and one woman into one flesh, and where the prophets and the apostles use that union as the figure of God and his people. Ephesians 5 quotes Genesis 2:24 and says outright, this is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.

Taken this way the book preaches to husbands harder than it flatters them. The love commanded in Ephesians is measured by a cross — even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it — and the headship it establishes is therefore a headship of self-expenditure, not of convenience. The dictionary holds the complementarian order Scripture teaches and holds with it the delight the Song teaches, and refuses the caricature that treats the first as incompatible with the second. Let thy fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.

pos: n. (a hard black wood; merchandise brought to Tyre by the men of Dedan)
etymology: From Greek ebenos through Latin, itself from an Egyptian word for the black heartwood. The Authorized Version uses it once, among the wares brought to Tyre.
biblical_def: The men of Dedan were thy merchants; many isles were the merchandise of thine hand: they brought thee for a present horns of ivory and ebony. The verse belongs to Ezekiel's roll call of the nations trading into Tyre, which reads like a customs ledger: Tarshish with silver, iron, tin, and lead; Javan, Tubal, and Meshech trading persons of men and vessels of brass; Togarmah with horses and mules; Syria with emeralds, purple, and fine linen; Judah and Israel with wheat, honey, oil, and balm; Dedan with ivory and ebony. The prophet is establishing how completely the world came to this one harbour. And then the fall: thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise, and in the day of thy ruin thy company shall fall into the midst of the seas. Ebony is a small item on a long manifest, and the manifest is the argument. A city can supply everything the world wants and still be a city the LORD is against, because the question Scripture asks of wealth is never how much but whose and to what end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a species of hard, heavy and durable wood, which admits of a fine polish or gloss, the best of which is jet black; in Scripture, merchandise brought to Tyre from Dedan.
webster_full: EBONY, n. A species of hard, heavy and durable wood, which admits of a fine polish or gloss.
DEDAN, n. A people and region of Arabia, descended from Abraham by Keturah, known for trade.
MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities.
TRAFFICK, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling.
COVETOUSNESS, n. A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good.
scriptures: The men of Dedan were thy merchants; many isles were the merchandise of thine hand: they brought thee for a present horns of ivory and ebony.
Tarshish was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of all kind of riches; with silver, iron, tin, and lead, they traded in thy fairs.
When thy wares went forth out of the seas, thou filledst many people; thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise.
Eze 28:2

Son of man, say unto the prince of Tyrus, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet thou art a man, and not God, though thou set thine heart as the heart of God:
corruption_summary: Prosperity is treated as self-evidently good and its sources left unexamined; Ezekiel's manifest includes ivory, ebony, and, a few verses earlier, the persons of men, and the whole ship goes down.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 27:13 is the line most readers pass over and it is the one that indicts the whole enterprise: Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market. Men listed between metals. Everything else in the chapter — the ivory, the ebony, the emeralds, the fine linen of Egypt, the blue and purple of Elishah — is genuinely beautiful, and the market that supplied it also trafficked in human beings. Scripture will not let the beauty of the goods settle the question about the market, and John repeats the same manifest in Revelation 18 with the same item last.

The chapter following names the root, and it is not economics. Because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet thou art a man, and not God, though thou set thine heart as the heart of God. Commercial pre-eminence had produced a theological claim. That is the trajectory Scripture watches for in wealth, and why covetousness is called idolatry rather than merely greed, and why the dictionary treats a nation's ledger as a spiritual document.

“thou didst enrich the kings of the earth” — the scale of the trade.
